title: Fall Risk Monitoring
answer: Fall risk monitoring covers systems that estimate how likely a patient is to fall and tools that alert staff when a fall may be happening. In hospitals it usually means predicting risk from the electronic health record, then acting on that score through bed alarms, chair sensors, or rounding schedules. In intensive care the same idea applies to sedated or delirious patients who try to get out of bed, and to those recovering mobility after long ventilation. It sits between nursing workflow, patient safety, and predictive analytics, and it is one of the more mature uses of prediction in hospital care.

sections.body: Fall risk monitoring covers systems that estimate how likely a patient is to fall and tools that alert staff when a fall may be happening. In hospitals it usually means predicting risk from the electronic health record, then acting on that score through bed alarms, chair sensors, or rounding schedules. In intensive care the same idea applies to sedated or delirious patients who try to get out of bed, and to those recovering mobility after long ventilation. It sits between nursing workflow, patient safety, and predictive analytics, and it is one of the more mature uses of prediction in hospital care.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on the hospital's existing record and monitoring estate rather than on dedicated hardware. Risk scores are computed from vitals, medications, mobility assessments, and nursing notes already stored in the electronic health record, and are surfaced in the chart or on a ward dashboard. Bed and chair sensors, pressure mats, and wearable tags feed a separate stream that triggers local alarms. Some deployments run the model on hospital servers, others through a vendor cloud, and a few use cameras with pose estimation in the room, which raises its own questions about what is recorded and who can see it.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The common approach is a supervised model trained on past falls and near misses, using features such as age, fall history, sedatives, anticoagulants, confusion scores, and mobility status. Older tools were simple checklists, and many wards still use them alongside a model. Newer work adds continuous sensing, so the system watches gait, bed exit attempts, and time since last assistance rather than scoring once per shift. Validation is difficult because falls are relatively rare, so a model can look accurate while missing most of the events that matter, and alert fatigue is a real operational constraint. Teams usually tune the threshold with nursing staff rather than on statistical grounds alone.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: A fall risk score is decision support, not a diagnosis, and responsibility for the patient stays with the clinical team. The main risks are missed falls when staff trust a low score, unnecessary restraints or alarms when they over react, and privacy concerns where cameras or continuous tracking are used. Documentation of model version, training data, and threshold changes matters if an event is later reviewed. This site tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, a reminder that clinical AI vendors can face litigation when a system fails. Any monitoring programme also has to fit the hospital's incident reporting and accreditation requirements.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is from periodic scoring toward continuous, ambient monitoring that combines the record with sensors and, in some pilots, computer vision. Better calibration and drift monitoring are likely to matter more than raw accuracy, because ward conditions change and a model trained on one unit may not transfer. Expect closer integration with nurse call systems and with mobility and delirium programmes rather than a standalone fall tool. Regulation and liability will shape adoption as much as the modelling does, and the field will keep negotiating how much automation a ward actually wants at three in the morning.
